1. Core Clinical Tension: A 52-year-old man presented with acute-onset dyspnea on exertion and dry cough, initially referred for suspected congestive heart failure. Instead of typical constitutional symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss), he exhibited acute right ventricular strain and severe precapillary pulmonary hypertension secondary to bilateral proximal pulmonary emboli occurring in the setting of an asymptomatic cavitary lung lesion.

2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage concludes after emergency clinical evaluation, baseline hematology and chemistry labs, negative lower extremity venous compression ultrasound, chest radiograph, 12-lead ECG, transthoracic echocardiogram, and contrast-enhanced thoracic CT angiography documenting bilateral pulmonary emboli and a right lung cavitary lesion. Confirmatory testing begins with invasive bronchial fibroscopy, aspirate smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture, and endobronchial biopsy.

3. Differential Distinctions: Left ventricular failure was excluded by normal left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 70%). Bronchogenic carcinoma was ruled out by histological absence of malignant cells on bronchial biopsy. Active mycobacterial infection was established by acid-fast smear positivity and culture from bronchial secretions, explaining both the pulmonary cavitary lesion and the secondary hypercoagulable state precipitating bilateral pulmonary thromboembolism.
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old previously healthy man was referred from a regional pulmonary center for the evaluation of suspected heart failure. He reported progressive shortness of breath on moderate exertion accompanied by a dry cough of two days' duration, which worsened at night. He denied fever, chills, unintentional weight loss, night sweats, chest pain, hemoptysis, or lower-extremity swelling. He had no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease or venous thromboembolism. His past medical history was notable only for documented exposure to an individual with chronic pulmonary infection ten years prior. He was a non-smoker and did not drink alcohol.

On physical examination, the patient was well-developed and in no acute distress. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 70 beats per minute, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, and temperature 36.9°C. Body mass index was 25.15 kg/m². Pulmonary auscultation revealed clear breath sounds bilaterally without crackles or wheezes. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated regular rate and rhythm without murmurs; there was no accentuation of the pulmonic component of the second heart sound, no jugular venous distention, and no peripheral edema.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 4,300/mm³, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and platelet count 315,000/mm³. Serum creatinine was 11.92 mg/L, fasting blood glucose 1.0 g/L, aspartate aminotransferase 19.9 IU/L, and alanine aminotransferase 15.6 IU/L. Inflammatory markers showed a C-reactive protein of 54.4 mg/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rates of 46 mm/hr and 59 mm/hr. The international normalized ratio (INR) was 1.10. HIV serology was negative. Compression ultrasonography of the lower extremities showed no evidence of deep venous thrombosis.

A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm, an incomplete right bundle branch block, and T-wave inversions across leads V1 through V3. Chest radiography revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette along with a right middle lobe cavitary lesion and regional lymphadenopathy. Transthoracic echocardiography showed dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, severe tricuspid regurgitation, severe pulmonary hypertension with an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 80 mmHg, and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 70%. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral proximal pulmonary emboli and confirmed a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Although referred for suspected heart failure due to dyspnea and cardiomegaly on chest radiograph, physical examination showed no jugular venous distention or peripheral edema, and echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 70%, identifying isolated right ventricular strain driven by pulmonary vascular obstruction.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ejection fraction of the left ventricle was 70%.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A pulmonary cavitary lesion with regional lymphadenopathy and acute pulmonary thromboembolism in a middle-aged adult raised suspicion for an underlying pulmonary malignancy; however, endobronchial biopsy of the lesion demonstrated severe epithelial dysplasia with an absence of carcinoma.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Brochial biopsy showed severe dysplasia of bronchial epithelium with absence of carcinoma.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Because of the unexplained cavitary lesion on thoracic imaging, bronchial fibroscopy with aspiration of bronchial secretions was performed; direct microscopy revealed numerous acid-fast bacilli and cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, establishing active pulmonary tuberculosis as the driving pathology inducing systemic inflammation and a secondary hypercoagulable state that triggered bilateral proximal pulmonary embolism.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Sputum was found to contain numerous acid-fast bacilli on direct microscopy (>15 bacilli/field). Culture results was positive for mycobacterium tuberculosis.

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case following Stanford MedCaseReasoning guidelines. Admission breakpoint strictly preserves clinical presentation, triage labs, bedside echocardiography, and thoracic CT angiography while withholding invasive bronchoscopy, acid-fast smear, cultures, and biopsy results.
